title: Izhikevich Model
intro: Izhikevich's 2003 model pairs a quadratic membrane equation with a linear recovery variable. With four parameters it reproduces about twenty firing patterns of cortical and thalamic neurons at roughly the cost of an LIF.

blocks.source:
dv/dt = 0.04 v^2 + 5 v + 140 - u + I
du/dt = a (b v - u)

if v >= 30 mV:   v <- c;   u <- u + d

blocks.text: v is the membrane potential in mV and t is in ms. u is a recovery variable that lumps together potassium activation and sodium inactivation; it feeds negatively back onto v. The quadratic term makes the upstroke of the spike regenerative: once v passes the unstable fixed point it runs away to the 30 mV peak, where it is cut and reset. The polynomial 0.04v^2 + 5v + 140 was fitted so that v is in mV and t in ms for cortical neurons.

items: a: time scale of u. Small a (0.02) means slow recovery; large a (0.1) means fast recovery, as in fast-spiking interneurons.
b: sensitivity of u to subthreshold v. b = 0.25 couples them more strongly, giving resonance and low-threshold spiking.
c: after-spike reset of v. A high reset (-50 mV) puts the neuron straight back near threshold, which produces bursts (chattering).
d: after-spike jump of u. Large d (8) gives strong spike-frequency adaptation; small d (2 or less) gives little.
Regular spiking (RS): a=0.02, b=0.2, c=-65, d=8. Excitatory pyramidal cells, with adaptation.
Intrinsically bursting (IB): c=-55, d=4. An initial burst, then single spikes.
Chattering (CH): c=-50, d=2. Repetitive high-frequency bursts (layer 2/3 cells).
Fast spiking (FS): a=0.1, b=0.2, c=-65, d=2. Inhibitory basket cells, no adaptation.
Low-threshold spiking (LTS): b=0.25. Inhibitory interneurons with rebound and adaptation.
Thalamo-cortical (TC): b=0.25, d=0.05. Tonic firing, or rebound bursts from hyperpolarization.
Resonator (RZ): a=0.1, b=0.26. Subthreshold oscillation; prefers inputs at its resonant frequency.

blocks.text: The step starts at 20 ms. In regular spiking mode the first interspike interval is short and later ones lengthen as u accumulates (adaptation). In fast spiking mode the rate is high and constant. Chattering produces tight bursts. Watch u (the second series): each spike kicks it up by d, and the spike train is shaped by how fast it decays.

Izhikevich's original code uses a 1 ms step with two 0.5 ms half-steps for v. For accuracy use 0.1-0.25 ms. Because the reset is triggered at 30 mV rather than at a true peak, the spike shape is not meaningful; only spike times are.

items: Pros: cheap (a few flops per step), rich behavior, famous large-scale demonstrations (Izhikevich and Edelman's 2008 thalamocortical model).
Cons: parameters are phenomenological, not biophysical; the quadratic blow-up makes accuracy step-size sensitive; and the fitted constants assume mV and ms units.
Relationship to other models: it is a quadratic integrate-and-fire neuron with adaptation, a close cousin of AdEx (#/snn/neuron-models/adex), which uses an exponential instead of a quadratic.

blocks.text: For a cortical column: use the RS preset for excitatory cells in layers 4 and 2/3, IB for layer 5 output cells, and FS for the inhibitory interneurons that implement the winner-take-all competition between minicolumns. One equation covers the whole column, which keeps a first prototype simple.

Sources: Izhikevich, "Simple model of spiking neurons" (IEEE Transactions on Neural Networks, 14(6), 2003); Izhikevich, "Which model to use for cortical spiking neurons?" (IEEE Transactions on Neural Networks, 15(5), 2004); Izhikevich & Edelman, "Large-scale model of mammalian thalamocortical systems" (PNAS, 2008).
